prompt.context: The railway company of Spain (RENFE), a former monopoly, is now opening to competition. RENFE has been divided into two separate companies: RENFE (train operation) and ADIF (company that manages the tracks, train stations and traffic control). A friend of yours has 90M € and has approached you for advice on starting a new train operation company to compete against the new RENFE. In particular, he wants to start by opening a new high speed train route between Madrid and Barcelona.
prompt.question: Should your friend go ahead and launch the business?

clarifying_info.q: How does the new company compare to RENFE on price?
clarifying_info.a: The new company is less expensive and more efficiently run; RENFE is very inefficient as a former monopoly.

clarifying_info.q: How does travel time compare to RENFE?
How does convenience compare to RENFE?
clarifying_info.a: Equally convenient — same stations and tracks (managed by ADIF).

clarifying_info.q: How long does a trip from Madrid to Barcelona take?
How many trips can we run per day?
clarifying_info.a: Two round trips per day, i.e., 4 trips per day total.

clarifying_info.q: How many trains do we need?
clarifying_info.a: Three operating trains plus one backup for breakdown, for a total of 4 trains.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of each train?
clarifying_info.a: 30M € per train (4 trains = 120M € total capital investment).

clarifying_info.q: What are annual operations and maintenance costs?
What is the train capacity and fare structure?
clarifying_info.a: Each train holds 500 people. At 40€: 95% occupancy; at 50€: 80% occupancy; at 60€: 60% occupancy.

clarifying_info.q: How long does the friend have to pay back the investment?

framework: Industry overview: Identify main competitors (RENFE, air travel) and assess competitive positioning on price, time, and convenience
Business overview: Map revenue streams (ticket sales primary; ancillary: food, ads) and cost structure (capex: trains; opex: marketing, operations/maintenance, personnel, IT)
Profitability analysis: Determine optimal ticket price via revenue per trip, then compute annual revenue and operating profit per train
Break-even / payback: Compare total operating profit against capital investment (4 trains × 30M €) over 10-year horizon
Recommendation: Advise go/no-go and surface options to improve economics

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — Industry: What does the competitive landscape look like, and does the new entrant have a viable position?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two main competitors: RENFE and air travel. Key comparison dimensions are price, travel time, and convenience. Strong answer notes: new entrant is cheaper and more efficient than RENFE; equal travel time and convenience (shared ADIF infrastructure). This suggests a potential opportunity worth quantifying.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Business: What are the main revenue streams and costs?
questions.guidance: Revenue: ticket sales (primary), onboard food and drinks, advertising on trains. For calculations focus on ticket revenue only. Costs: capital expenditure (train purchase), marketing, operations and maintenance, personnel, IT. Candidate should note the operating model — 4 trips per day, 3 active trains plus 1 backup.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Pricing: At which ticket price (40€, 50€, or 60€) is revenue per trip maximised?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute revenue per trip at each price point and identify the optimum.

math.setup: Revenue per trip = ticket price × occupancy rate × capacity (500 seats)
math.answer: Optimal price is 50€, yielding 20,000 € per trip — highest of the three options.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Profitability: What is the estimated annual operating profit?
questions.guidance: Using the 50€ price, candidate calculates annual revenue then subtracts annual operating costs. Note: costs are per train; the backup (4th) train does not operate, so only 3 trains' worth of opex applies. Annual opex per operating train = 15M (marketing) + 10M (operations) = 25M €.

math.setup: Annual revenue = 365 days × 4 trips/day × 20,000 €/trip. Operating cost = 25M € per operating train × 3 trains.
steps: Operating profit per train: 29.2M − 25M = 4.2M € per train
Total operating profit (3 active trains): 4.2M × 3 = 12.6M € per year
math.answer: Estimated annual operating profit is approximately 12.6M €.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 — Payback: How long does it take to recoup the capital investment? Is the 10-year target met?
questions.guidance: Capital investment = 4 trains × 30M € = 120M €. At 12.6M € profit per year the payback period is roughly 9.5 years, just under the 10-year limit. However, the friend only has 90M €, which covers only 3 trains, not 4 — this is a critical gap. Candidate should flag the funding shortfall.

math.setup: Payback = total capex / annual operating profit
math.answer: ~9.5 years — barely within 10 years, but the friend's 90M € budget is insufficient to buy 4 trains (need 120M €).

brainstorming.prompt: What options could make the business more profitable or address the funding gap?

categories.name: Capital / Funding
ideas: Lease trains instead of buying to reduce upfront capex
Seek a joint venture with a foreign rail operator that has excess capacity
Raise additional equity or debt financing to cover the 30M € shortfall

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Introduce premium / business class seating at higher fares
Grow ancillary revenue from onboard food, beverages, and retail
Sell advertising space on trains and in stations
Add loyalty programme to increase repeat ridership

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Negotiate volume discounts on train procurement
Optimise scheduling to reduce idle train time
Outsource non-core functions (catering, maintenance) to lower opex

categories.name: Strategic Options
ideas: Start with fewer routes or trips to reduce risk before scaling
Partner with ADIF for preferential track access pricing
Target underserved secondary city-pairs beyond Madrid–Barcelona

recommendation: Under current circumstances the friend should NOT invest: the 90M € budget covers only 3 trains while 4 are required, creating a 30M € funding gap before operations even begin
Even with 4 trains the payback period (~9.5 years) leaves very little margin against the 10-year target, with no buffer for cost overruns or lower-than-expected occupancy
risks: Occupancy may not reach 80% if RENFE responds with price cuts or service improvements
Capital costs could escalate; maintenance and operating costs are estimates
Regulatory risk: new entrant in a liberalised but formerly state-controlled market
Fuel/energy price increases could erode the thin operating margin
next_steps: Explore train leasing to eliminate or reduce the 120M € capex
Assess feasibility of a JV with a foreign operator to share capital and operational risk
Model downside scenarios at lower occupancy rates (e.g., 60–70%) to stress-test payback
Conduct detailed demand study for the Madrid–Barcelona corridor before committing capital
